case_title: Prosecutor v. Galić — terror against the civilian population
question: Did the campaign of sniping and shelling against the besieged city constitute the crime of terror against the civilian population, as a violation of the laws or customs of war?
facts: Over a period of approximately 23 months, forces under the accused's command conducted sniping and shelling attacks against civilian areas of a besieged city. The attacks struck civilians going about daily activities — queuing for water, attending funerals, crossing intersections. The attacks were not isolated incidents but a sustained campaign, which included attacks with no identifiable military objective in the vicinity; taken as a whole, the campaign had no discernible significance in military terms. The accused ordered the campaign and facilitated and encouraged it; he held effective command over the forces conducting the attacks and received regular reports on their activities. By an agreement of 22 May 1992, the parties to the conflict had brought Article 51 of Additional Protocol I into effect between themselves.
holding: The Trial Chamber, by majority, found the accused guilty under Article 3 of the Statute of acts of violence the primary purpose of which is to spread terror among the civilian population, as set forth in Article 51 of Additional Protocol I. It founded jurisdiction over that crime on Article 51 of Additional Protocol I, which the parties had brought into effect between themselves by an agreement of 22 May 1992. It found that the accused ordered the campaign of attacks and convicted him under Article 7(1) of the Statute only. (Customary criminal liability for the prohibition of terror was later affirmed by the Appeals Chamber, by majority, in 2006; it is not the Trial Chamber's ground.)
confidence_reasoning: The law is settled: Article 51(2) AP I expressly prohibits acts of violence the primary purpose of which is to spread terror among civilians, and Article 8(2)(b)(i) Rome Statute criminalizes intentionally directing attacks against the civilian population. The facts as given — a sustained 23-month campaign against civilians with no military objectives or discernible military significance — are a paradigmatic instance of terror tactics. The parties had brought Article 51 AP I into effect by agreement. No genuine legal or factual contest exists on these points.

verdict.conclusion: Yes. The campaign of sniping and shelling against the besieged city constituted the crime of terror against the civilian population as a violation of the laws and customs of war. The sustained, 23-month campaign directed at civilians engaged in daily activities — with no identifiable military objectives and no discernible military significance — demonstrates that the primary purpose was to spread terror among the civilian population, prohibited by Article 51(2) of Additional Protocol I (brought into effect between the parties by agreement of 22 May 1992) and criminalized as a war crime under Article 8(2)(b)(i) of the Rome Statute. The accused's effective command, direct ordering of the campaign, and receipt of regular reports establish individual criminal responsibility. The attacks also independently violated the prohibitions on indiscriminate attacks (Article 51(4)(a) AP I) and disproportionate attacks (Article 57(2)(a)(iii) AP I).
verdict.reasoning: All three arguments survive unchallenged because no objections were filed. Argument 1 directly establishes the terror crime under Article 51(2) AP I and Article 8(2)(b)(i) Rome Statute. The factual pattern — attacks on civilians queuing for water, attending funerals, crossing intersections, over 23 months, with no military objectives or advantage — satisfies the 'primary purpose to spread terror' standard. Argument 2 reinforces this with independent violations of distinction and proportionality. Argument 3 establishes the accused's command responsibility. All cited authorities are resolved against the corpus.

arguments.claim: The sustained campaign of sniping and shelling was an act whose primary purpose was to spread terror among the civilian population, thereby violating Article 51(2) of Additional Protocol I and constituting a war crime under Article 8(2)(b)(i) of the Rome Statute.
arguments.reasoning: Article 51(2) of AP I expressly prohibits "Acts or threats of violence the primary purpose of which is to spread terror among the civilian population". The factual pattern shows attacks were directed at civilians engaged in everyday activities, with no identifiable military objective and no discernible military advantage, indicating the primary purpose was to intimidate and terrorise the population. Such intentional directing of attacks against civilians is captured by the Rome Statute provision that criminalises "Intentionally directing attacks against the civilian population as such or against individual civilians not taking direct part in hostilities". Accordingly, the campaign satisfies the elements of the prohibited act under both treaty sources and thus amounts to a war crime.

arguments.claim: The attacks were indiscriminate because they were not directed at specific military objectives and were disproportionate, violating the distinction and proportionality rules of Article 51(4) and the precautionary obligations of Article 57 of Additional Protocol I.
arguments.reasoning: Article 51(4)(a) defines indiscriminate attacks as those "that are not directed at a specific military objective". The campaign repeatedly struck civilians queuing for water, attending funerals and crossing intersections, locations that lacked any military function. Moreover, Article 57(2)(a)(iii) obliges commanders to refrain from attacks expected to cause incidental civilian loss that would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. The factual record shows the campaign had no discernible military significance, so any civilian harm was clearly excessive. Consequently, the attacks breach both the distinction and proportionality principles, constituting war crimes under the Rome Statute’s provisions on indiscriminate attacks.

arguments.claim: The accused commander is individually criminally responsible for the war crimes because he ordered, facilitated and had effective control over the forces that carried out the terror campaign, satisfying the doctrine of command responsibility.
arguments.reasoning: Command responsibility imposes liability on superiors who, having effective control, knew or should have known about the commission of war crimes and failed to prevent or punish them. The facts state that the accused ordered the campaign, received regular reports, and exercised effective command over the forces. By directing an unlawful campaign that violates Article 51(2) and the proportionality rules, the commander meets the actus reus of the underlying war crime (Article 8(2)(b)(i) of the Rome Statute). His superior position and knowledge satisfy the mens rea element of command responsibility, rendering him individually liable.
